sheet-1-1.description: The centre of Branchville as it stood in May 1920, drawn at 100 feet to an inch with north to the right of the page, so that Main Street runs up the sheet towards the west-north-west. The part covers Main and Church streets from the north-west edge of the sheet down to the junction with Broad Street, Madison Avenue and Wantage Avenue, and the blocks between Roseville Avenue, Price, Gladstone Avenue and the lower Main Street towards the Culver Creek bridge. Most frontages along Main and Church are dwellings and small stores, with a denser commercial group on Main near Horseshoe Place: stores, a drug store, a hardware store with a hall above, a general store, flats, a livery and a blacksmith shop. The Presbyterian church stands at the head of Wantage Avenue. On the west side Culver Creek is dammed by wooden and earthen dams into Electric Lake, beside which stand the ice houses of Borden's Farm Products Co. with an ice conveyor, a garage with buried gasoline tanks, and the electric light plant below the Roseville Avenue plank bridge. A concrete bridge carries Gladstone Avenue over the creek. East of Main the sheet is mostly open land in large lots along Madison Avenue, New Street and Wantage Avenue, with scattered dwellings and outbuildings; a dash-dot match line marks the edge of sheet 2. Water mains and their sizes, hydrants and street widths are given throughout. The sheet carries the title cartouche, key, water and fire notes and a New Jersey location map (outside this part), and an inset of the area half a mile north-west of the post office, which is a separate part.
notes: Main (north of the Church junction) is modern Main Street; Church is Church Hill Road; Main between Church and Madison Avenue is the west end of modern Broad Street
Main St. running south-east from the Broad Street junction is modern Mill Street
Roseville Avenue is modern Kemah Lake Road; Gladstone Avenue is modern Hillside Avenue; Madison Avenue is modern Mattison Avenue; Price is Price Avenue; New is New Street
Horseshoe Place is not in the modern street data
Borden's Farm Products Co. ice houses on Electric Lake; electric light plant on Culver Creek
Main and Church meet at a shallow angle; that junction and Gladstone Avenue / Main St. were not detected and are not control points

sheet-2-1.description: The eastern half of Branchville in May 1920, drawn at 100 feet to an inch with north about 24 degrees right of up. The part runs from the junction of Broad Street, Main Street, Madison Street and Wantage Avenue at its upper left, along Wantage Avenue past New and Maple, and along Broad and Main (the modern Mill Street) south-east to Lloyd Avenue, Private Lane and Fox Hill Road beyond Dry Brook. Broad is the business street: hotels, the post office, stores, a plumber, the M.E. church and parsonage near its west end, then dwellings on narrow lots. Between Broad and Main lie Roe Avenue and Milk Street; Main follows the shore of Crisman Pond, with stores and dwellings, and crosses Culver Creek on a plank bridge near the steel bridge of Milk Street. The Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad occupies the middle of the sheet: station, freight platform, turntable, scattered piles of railroad ties, coal trestle and coal bins, with Railroad Avenue and Maple along its east side. Industry includes the Branchville Silk Mills (silk weaving, machinery being installed), a feed and supply house, feed house, lumber sheds and the milk station and bottling plant of Borden's Farm Products Co. with its ice houses and an ice chute from Crisman Pond. A public school stands on Wantage Avenue. The south-west of the sheet along Morris Avenue and Newton Avenue is open land with scattered dwellings. Dry Brook crosses the east side with plank and concrete bridges. A heavy-bordered inset at upper left, a separate part, continues Main south of the Dry Brook bridge.
notes: Main (south-east of the Broad Street junction) is modern Mill Street; Madison Street is Mattison Avenue; Roe Avenue is Division Street; Milk is Milk Street; Maple and Railroad Avenue are Maple Avenue and Railroad Avenue
Clairmont Place and Private Lane were not identified in the modern street data; Private Lane may be the modern 1st Street
Broad / Fox Hill Road was detected about 14 m from the fit to the other junctions and was left out; the part south-east of Dry Brook rests on Broad / Lloyd Avenue alone
Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad station, turntable and coal trestle; the line is now the Sussex Branch Trail
Branchville Silk Mills; Borden's Farm Products Co. milk station

sheet-2-2.description: A small inset in a heavy border at the upper left of sheet 2, drawn at the sheet's scale of 100 feet to an inch and in the sheet's orientation. It continues Main (the modern Mill Street) south from the plank bridge over Dry Brook, where the main map of sheet 2 ends, for about 600 feet. The Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad runs parallel on the west side of the street, crossing Dry Brook on a trestle beside the road bridge. The blocks either side of Main carry a handful of frame dwellings with outbuildings, auto garages, a chicken house and coops, and a small store; house numbers run from 225 to 261. A four-inch water pipe runs down Main, with one hydrant. The block numbers 35 and 38 are printed in the blocks, and the edges of the inset are marked No Exposure. The rest of the inset is open land.
notes: Placed from one point, the plank bridge over Dry Brook drawn on both this inset and the main map of sheet 2, with the scale and rotation of the main map: low confidence
